items.prose: Insufficient cooling rate during oil quench left 28% retained austenite in the carburized case. Under 400 horsepower load in the turbine reduction gearbox, the soft phase transformed into untempered martensite, causing severe surface spalling along the pitch line.

Excessive carburizing time (eighteen hours at 930°C) completely through-carburized the narrow 4mm gear teeth. Lacking a ductile, shock-absorbing core, three consecutive gear teeth snapped off at the root fillet during pump startup.

A leaking water cooling coil introduced 3% water into the sixty-barrel quench oil tank. Water droplets touching the 850°C ring gear caused violent steam cavitation and localized thermal shock, fracturing the 600mm gear ring into three pieces.

Failure of the quench tank mechanical agitator impeller created non-uniform vapor blanket cooling across the gear face. The 450mm bevel gear distorted into an oval shape with 3.4mm radial runout, rendering tooth contact pattern un-meshable.

Furnace door air leak allowed oxidizing flue gases to burn carbon out of the gear surface during the three-hour austenitizing soak. A 0.4mm layer of dead-soft ferrite covered the teeth; gear profile wore out in forty-eight hours of operation.

High dew-point endothermic gas atmosphere produced internal oxidation of chromium and manganese to a depth of 25 microns along prior austenite grain boundaries. Microscopic root notches triggered rapid bending fatigue cracks under crane hoist shock loads.

Excess nitrogen potential in the liquid salt bath produced an overly thick 35-micron epsilon-iron nitride 'compound layer' on the tooth flanks. The brittle glass-like white layer flaked off during engine break-in, contaminating the lube oil with diamond-hard abrasive particles.
